transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Let's get started. As you know, we're here to plan our initial defense strategy in the trade secrets misappropriation case filed by the former employee. The complaint seeks broad inspection of our devices and systems, and we need to be ready to address that well before the case-management conference next month. Our priorities are clear: protect the company's confidential information and keep defense costs controlled. I need discovery counsel and insurance-coverage counsel to identify any facts that should shape our initial defense plan before I approve it. Let's start with discovery counsel — what do we need to know to build our discovery framework?

transcript.text: I need to share a key finding from my forensic review. I examined the former employee's company laptop and confirmed that exactly three identified trade-secret files were copied to the device. Critically, I found no customer data on the device and no evidence of any additional copying beyond those three files. My forensic report is currently awaiting final partner review and has not yet been added to the case plan. This should significantly shape our discovery strategy — it narrows the scope of what the plaintiff can realistically claim was taken and gives us strong grounds to push back against the broad inspection demands in the complaint.

transcript.text: I need to flag several insurance-coverage constraints that will directly shape our defense plan. I've reviewed the applicable policy endorsement, and here's what it requires: the trade-secret defense is covered, but subject to a $75,000 self-insured retention. We must use insurer-approved panel counsel. We need written insurer consent before any forensic vendor is engaged — that's critical given Samir's forensic work. And we must notify the insurer as part of the approved defense plan. The endorsement itself is stored in the risk department's file and has not yet been attached to this matter. Elena, I'd recommend we address the panel-counsel requirement and the forensic-vendor consent issue before you approve the plan, though I understand we can commit to resolving certain administrative and coverage follow-up items after the meeting.
